stem:
Stimulus: Glucose and fructose are monosaccharides with the same molecular formula, C6H12O6, but their atoms are arranged differently, so the two molecules have different three-dimensional shapes. A transport protein in the plasma membrane of intestinal cells moves fructose across the membrane much more efficiently than it moves glucose.

Question: Which statement best explains why a transport protein can distinguish between these two sugars?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They have different numbers of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms, so the protein recognizes the sugar with more atoms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They differ in the number of hydroxyl groups attached to the sugar backbone, and the protein recognizes the extra groups.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They have the same atoms arranged differently, which gives them different three-dimensional shapes that fit the transport protein differently.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fructose is a polysaccharide, so it must be moved by a different kind of transport protein than glucose.

stem:
Stimulus: Sickle cell disease results from a single amino acid substitution in β-globin: glutamic acid (polar, negatively charged at pH 7.4) at position 6 is replaced by valine (nonpolar, hydrophobic). Under low-oxygen conditions, sickle hemoglobin (HbS) polymerizes into rigid fibers that deform red blood cells. Normal hemoglobin (HbA) does not polymerize under the same conditions.

Question: Which best explains the molecular basis for HbS polymerization under low-oxygen conditions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Valine's smaller side chain leaves a gap that destabilizes β-globin's alpha-helix, unfolding HbS into fibers

choices.label: B
choices.text: The hydrophobic valine at position 6 inserts into the complementary hydrophobic pocket exposed on adjacent deoxygenated HbS molecules, driving chain polymerization through hydrophobic interactions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Valine disrupts the disulfide bonds that normally maintain hemoglobin's quaternary structure, causing uncontrolled aggregation

choices.label: D
choices.text: The loss of glutamic acid's negative charge at position 6 directly prevents HbS from binding oxygen, causing polymerization as an indirect consequence

stem:
Stimulus: Two cells are compared under electron microscopy. Cell 1 is approximately 2 μm in diameter, has a single circular chromosome in the cytoplasm, 70S ribosomes, no membrane-bound organelles, and a peptidoglycan cell wall. Cell 2 is approximately 20 μm in diameter, has multiple linear chromosomes within a double-membrane nucleus, 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm, mitochondria, and an endoplasmic reticulum.

Question: Which conclusion about cell classification is most directly supported by the observations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cell 1 is eukaryotic because having a peptidoglycan cell wall shows that it has specialized extracellular structures.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cell 2 is prokaryotic because mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum are involved in energy processing and protein transport rather than in storing genetic information.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cell 1 is prokaryotic and Cell 2 is eukaryotic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both cells are eukaryotic because both contain ribosomes, and ribosomes are membrane-bound organelles used for protein synthesis.

stem:
Stimulus: A student places strips of celery into three solutions for 30 minutes: (1) distilled water, (2) dilute salt solution, and (3) concentrated salt solution. After 30 minutes, the strip in distilled water is rigid and crisp; the strip in dilute salt solution is slightly flexible; the strip in concentrated salt solution is limp and wilted. The student notes that unlike red blood cells placed in distilled water, the celery does not burst.

Question: Which best explains why celery in distilled water becomes rigid rather than lysing, unlike animal cells in hypotonic solution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cellulose cell wall resists expansion after water enters, so rising turgor pressure limits further swelling and prevents lysis.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The plant plasma membrane becomes impermeable to water in distilled water, so the cell wall remains rigid because no osmosis occurs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Water enters until the cytoplasm becomes isotonic with the surrounding water, at which point net movement stops and the cell stays intact.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Plant cells avoid lysis because their cytoplasm is always isotonic to distilled water, while animal cells are hypertonic to distilled water.

stem:
Stimulus: Liver cells take up LDL cholesterol by endocytosis. LDL particles bind to LDL receptors, which are proteins in the plasma membrane. The membrane then folds inward and engulfs the bound LDL in a vesicle that carries it into the cell. In familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), mutations eliminate functional LDL receptors from the cell surface.

Question: Which prediction about individuals with familial hypercholesterolemia is best supported by the described process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Their liver cells will compensate by taking in large amounts of LDL through nonspecific endocytosis that does not need receptors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: LDL particles will accumulate in the bloodstream because liver cells cannot specifically recognize and take them in without functional receptors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Their liver cells will take in LDL normally, because endocytosis does not depend on any proteins in the plasma membrane.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Their liver cells will collect LDL inside vesicles, because the vesicles cannot fuse with the plasma membrane to release it.

stem:
Stimulus: Pancreatic cells secrete the digestive enzyme amylase. Amylase is made by ribosomes on the rough ER. It is then modified and packaged in the Golgi complex, and transport vesicles carry it to the plasma membrane to be secreted. A researcher treats the cells with a drug that blocks the formation of the transport vesicles that carry material from the rough ER to the Golgi complex.

Question: Which outcome for amylase in the treated cells is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amylase is no longer made at all, because ribosomes on the rough ER cannot make proteins unless vesicles leave the ER.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Amylase is made by ribosomes in the Golgi complex instead, and it is then secreted normally.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Amylase is still made on the rough ER, but it builds up there, and little reaches the Golgi complex or is secreted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Amylase is secreted faster than normal, because it no longer has to pass through the Golgi complex first.

stem:
Stimulus: Evidence supporting the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria includes: (1) mitochondria have a double membrane, with an inner membrane that resembles the plasma membrane of a prokaryote and an outer membrane that resembles the endomembrane of the eukaryotic cell; (2) mitochondria have their own circular DNA, like the chromosome of a prokaryote; (3) mitochondria make some of their own proteins on their own ribosomes; (4) new mitochondria arise from existing mitochondria without the cell having to divide.

Question: Which single piece of evidence most specifically supports the claim that a prokaryote was engulfed by a host cell, rather than simply showing a prokaryote-like ancestry?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The double membrane, with an outer layer like host endomembrane and an inner layer like a prokaryotic plasma membrane, matches a prokaryote surrounded by a host membrane.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Having its own circular DNA shows that mitochondria can still survive on their own outside the host cell, as a free-living prokaryote would.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Making new mitochondria without any cell division shows that mitochondria were once free-living prokaryotes that lived on their own.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Having their own ribosomes for making proteins shows that mitochondria are currently prokaryotes that live inside eukaryotic cells.

stem:
Stimulus: Researchers study two proteins from red blood cells. Protein M is found with the membranes of broken cells and cannot be separated from the phospholipids unless the bilayer is dissolved. The amino acids on the surface of Protein M have mostly nonpolar R groups. Protein C is found dissolved in the cytoplasm. The amino acids on the surface of Protein C have mostly polar R groups.

Question: Which characterization of Protein M is best supported by these results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A protein dissolved in the cytoplasm, with nonpolar R groups on its surface that interact with the surrounding water.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A protein attached only to the outside of the membrane, with its nonpolar R groups facing the watery environment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A protein embedded in the membrane, with polar R groups on the surface that touches the phospholipid tails.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A protein embedded in the bilayer, with nonpolar R groups on the surface that touches the hydrophobic tails of the phospholipids.

stem:
Stimulus: Glucose and galactose are monosaccharides with the same molecular formula, C6H12O6, but their atoms are arranged differently, so the two molecules have different three-dimensional shapes. A transport protein in the plasma membrane of a bacterium moves galactose into the cell efficiently but moves glucose across the membrane very poorly.

Question: Which statement best explains how this transport protein can distinguish between the two sugars?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glucose is a polysaccharide, so it is too large to fit through the transport protein that moves galactose.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Galactose has hydroxyl groups that glucose lacks, and the transport protein recognizes those extra groups on galactose.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Galactose contains more carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms than glucose, so the transport protein holds on to it more strongly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The two sugars have the same atoms arranged differently, so their shapes differ and only galactose fits the transport protein.

stem:
Stimulus: Yeast cells have a transport protein in the plasma membrane that moves sugar A into the cell efficiently but moves sugar B very poorly. Sugars A and B are monosaccharides with the same molecular formula, C6H12O6, but their atoms are arranged differently. A third monosaccharide, sugar C, also has the formula C6H12O6. Its atoms are arranged so that its molecule has nearly the same three-dimensional shape as sugar A.

Question: Which prediction about the transport of sugar C is best supported by this information?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sugar C will be moved efficiently only after it is broken down into smaller molecules by hydrolysis first.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sugar C will be moved into the cells efficiently, because its three-dimensional shape is nearly the same as sugar A's.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sugar C will be moved as poorly as sugar B, because all three sugars have the same molecular formula.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sugar C will be moved poorly, because it has a different molecular formula from the formula of sugar A.

stem:
Stimulus: A soluble bacterial enzyme normally stays dissolved even at high concentration. A mutant form has a single amino acid substitution in which a surface-exposed threonine (polar, uncharged) is replaced by isoleucine (nonpolar, hydrophobic). At high concentration the mutant enzyme forms insoluble clumps, while the normal enzyme does not. Both forms fold into the same overall three-dimensional shape and are fully active when dissolved.

Question: Which best explains why the mutant enzyme forms clumps?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Isoleucine's larger side chain disrupts the enzyme's overall fold, so the mutant partly unfolds and tangles with other enzyme molecules in solution.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Isoleucine forms ionic bonds between separate enzyme molecules, linking them together in a way that threonine cannot.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The substitution damages the enzyme's catalytic site, and the resulting loss of activity makes the protein precipitate out of solution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The exposed nonpolar isoleucine side chains on different enzyme molecules associate through hydrophobic interactions, away from the surrounding water.

stem:
Stimulus: A therapeutic protein tends to clump when stored at high concentration. The clumping occurs through contacts between nonpolar leucine side chains that are exposed on the protein's surface. Engineers make a single substitution that replaces one of these surface leucines with glutamate (negatively charged at physiological pH). The modified protein folds into the same shape and stays dissolved at high concentration.

Question: Which best explains why the substitution reduces clumping?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glutamate is also nonpolar, so it strengthens the hydrophobic core and stabilizes the protein against clumping.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glutamate's charged side chain interacts with water and repels neighboring proteins, which removes a nonpolar contact that held molecules together.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glutamate forms covalent peptide bonds with neighboring proteins that lock each protein into a single compact shape.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glutamate makes the protein fold into a smaller shape that buries its other nonpolar groups in the interior.

stem:
Stimulus: Two photosynthetic cells are compared under electron microscopy. Cell 1 is approximately 3 μm in diameter and has a single circular chromosome in the cytoplasm and photosynthetic pigments embedded in folded internal membranes. It has no nucleus and no chloroplasts. Cell 2 is approximately 12 μm in diameter and has multiple linear chromosomes inside a double-membrane nucleus and chloroplasts.

Question: Which conclusion about cell classification is most directly supported by the observations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both cells are eukaryotic because both are photosynthetic and both contain DNA.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cell 1 is eukaryotic because it carries out photosynthesis on internal membranes, which only organelles can provide.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cell 2 is prokaryotic because chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, a process that bacteria also perform.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cell 1 is prokaryotic because it has no nucleus, and Cell 2 is eukaryotic because it has a nucleus and membrane-bound chloroplasts.

stem:
Stimulus: A microscopist compares two single-celled organisms. Organism 1 is approximately 1 μm long and has one circular chromosome in a region of cytoplasm with no surrounding membrane, a small circular plasmid, and a peptidoglycan cell wall. Organism 2 is approximately 6 μm in diameter and has linear chromosomes enclosed in a nuclear envelope, mitochondria, and a cell wall made of chitin.

Question: Which conclusion about how these organisms should be classified is most directly supported by the observations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Organism 1 is prokaryotic because its DNA lacks a surrounding membrane, and Organism 2 is eukaryotic because it has a nucleus.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both organisms are prokaryotic because both are single-celled, and single-celled organisms are always prokaryotes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Organism 2 is prokaryotic because it has a cell wall, just as Organism 1 does, and cell walls are a prokaryotic feature.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Organism 1 is eukaryotic because it has two separate DNA molecules, the main chromosome and a small plasmid, in the same cell.

stem:
Stimulus: A student weighs potato cores before and after placing them in solutions for 60 minutes. A core in distilled water gains 9% in mass and becomes stiff. A core in 0.2 M sucrose changes very little in mass. A core in 0.8 M sucrose loses 18% of its mass and becomes limp. The student notes that the core in distilled water stops gaining mass after about 45 minutes and that its cells do not burst.

Question: Which best explains why the core in distilled water stops gaining mass and its cells do not burst?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Water keeps entering until the solute concentration inside the cells equals that of distilled water, and then net movement stops.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The plasma membranes of the potato cells become impermeable to water once the core is stiff, so osmosis stops.

choices.label: C
choices.text: As water enters, the cell wall resists expansion and turgor pressure rises until it opposes further net water entry.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Potato cells have the same solute concentration as distilled water, so they neither gain nor lose water.

stem:
Stimulus: A student mounts onion epidermal tissue in distilled water and views it under a microscope. The cells are firm, and the plasma membrane presses against the cell wall. The student replaces the water with a 1 M salt solution. Within minutes the cells shrink, and in the corners of each cell the plasma membrane pulls away from the cell wall, leaving gaps. The plasma membrane remains intact.

Question: Which best explains why the plasma membrane pulls away from the cell wall in the salt solution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cell wall contracts when it contacts the salt solution and pulls itself away from the plasma membrane.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Water leaves the cells by osmosis toward the more concentrated solution, so the cell contents shrink while the rigid wall keeps its shape.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Salt enters the cells and dissolves the cell wall, which releases the plasma membrane from its surface.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Active transport pumps water out of the cells against its concentration gradient, which shrinks the cell contents.

stem:
Stimulus: Developing red blood cells take in iron by endocytosis. Iron-bound transferrin, a protein in the blood, binds to transferrin receptors, which are proteins in the plasma membrane. The membrane then folds inward and engulfs the bound transferrin in a vesicle that carries the iron into the cell. A rare inherited mutation prevents transferrin receptors from reaching the plasma membrane of developing red blood cells.

Question: Which prediction about individuals with this mutation is best supported by the described process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Iron-bound transferrin will stay in the blood at high levels, because the cells have no receptors to bind it and take it in.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cells will have more iron available inside, because the iron stays outside the cells, where it can diffuse freely into the cytoplasm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron-bound transferrin will cross the phospholipid bilayer by simple diffusion instead, because the receptors are not needed for uptake.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The plasma membrane will stop folding inward in these cells, so no other substance can be taken in by endocytosis.

stem:
Stimulus: Liver cells remove LDL particles, which carry cholesterol, from the blood by endocytosis. LDL binds to receptor proteins in the plasma membrane, and the binding makes the membrane fold inward and engulf the LDL in a vesicle. A mutant form of the receptor reaches the plasma membrane and binds LDL as well as the normal receptor does, but it cannot make the membrane fold inward.

Question: Which prediction about liver cells that have only the mutant receptor is best supported by the described process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cells will take in LDL normally, because binding to the receptor is the only step in uptake that needs a receptor protein.

choices.label: B
choices.text: LDL will bind to the surface of the cells but will not be taken in, so the level of LDL in the blood will stay high.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fewer receptors will reach the plasma membrane, so the cells will bind less LDL than normal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: LDL will cross the phospholipid bilayer directly once it is bound to the receptor, so the level of LDL in the blood will fall.

stem:
Stimulus: Pancreatic cells secrete the digestive enzyme amylase. Normally, amylase is made by ribosomes attached to the rough ER, and it then passes through the Golgi complex and transport vesicles before it is secreted from the cell. A researcher treats the cells with a drug that stops ribosomes from attaching to the rough ER. The ribosomes remain in the cytoplasm.

Question: Which outcome for amylase in the treated cells is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amylase moves directly from the cytoplasm into the Golgi complex, where it is modified and then secreted as usual.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Amylase is no longer made at all, because only ribosomes attached to the rough ER can carry out protein synthesis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Amylase is still made, but in the cytoplasm rather than at the rough ER, so it does not enter the endomembrane system and little is secreted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Amylase is made on the smooth ER instead and is secreted normally, because the smooth ER also takes part in making proteins.

stem:
Stimulus: A pancreatic cell secretes a digestive enzyme. Researchers expose the cells briefly to radioactive amino acids and then follow the radioactive enzyme over time. At first, most of the radioactivity is found in the rough ER. Later it is found in the Golgi complex, then in transport vesicles near the plasma membrane, and finally outside the cell.

Question: Which interpretation of these results is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The smooth ER makes the enzyme, because the rough ER only provides support for the cell and does not take part in making proteins.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ribosomes on the rough ER make the enzyme, and it then moves through the Golgi complex and vesicles, where it is modified and packaged for secretion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Golgi complex makes the enzyme from mRNA, and the rough ER later folds it before the enzyme is moved to the plasma membrane.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lysosomes receive the enzyme from the rough ER and release it from the cell, because lysosomes are the organelles that secrete enzymes.

stem:
Stimulus: Evidence supporting the endosymbiotic origin of chloroplasts includes: (1) chloroplasts have a double membrane, with an inner membrane like the plasma membrane of a cyanobacterium and an outer membrane like the host cell's endomembrane; (2) chloroplasts contain their own circular DNA; (3) chloroplasts contain ribosomes made of rRNA and protein, like those of prokaryotes; (4) chloroplasts reproduce independently of the cell cycle of the host.

Question: Which single piece of evidence most specifically supports the claim that a host cell engulfed a cyanobacterium, rather than only showing that chloroplasts have a prokaryote-like ancestry?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reproducing independently of the host's cell cycle shows that the chloroplast was surrounded by a host membrane during engulfment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The double membrane, with an inner layer like a cyanobacterial membrane and an outer layer like host endomembrane, matches engulfment by a host vesicle.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Having its own circular DNA shows that chloroplasts are still able to survive on their own outside the plant cell.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Having ribosomes made of rRNA and protein shows that each chloroplast is still a free-living cyanobacterium inside the cell.

stem:
Stimulus: Two hypotheses explain the origin of chloroplasts. In the endosymbiosis hypothesis, a host cell engulfed a cyanobacterium. In the infolding hypothesis, part of the host's own plasma membrane folded inward and enclosed some of the host's cytoplasm, which later specialized for photosynthesis. Researchers sequence the chloroplast genome and compare it with other genomes. They find that chloroplast genes are circular, lack histones, and are more similar in sequence to genes of modern cyanobacteria than to genes in the plant's own nucleus.

Question: Which conclusion is best supported by the sequence comparison?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because chloroplasts have a double membrane, the sequence data show that they formed by infolding of the host's plasma membrane.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because chloroplasts carry their own DNA, the sequence data show that the host nucleus contributes no genes to chloroplast function.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chloroplast genes are more closely related to cyanobacterial genes than to the host's nuclear genes, which supports endosymbiosis over infolding of the host's membrane.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because chloroplast DNA lacks histones, the sequence data show that chloroplasts are not part of the plant cell.

stem:
Stimulus: Protein X is embedded in the plasma membrane of an intestinal cell and extends across it. A segment in the middle of Protein X is made of amino acids with nonpolar (hydrophobic) R groups. The segments at each end of Protein X are made of amino acids with polar (hydrophilic) R groups.

Question: Which arrangement of Protein X in the membrane is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The nonpolar middle segment lies in the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer, and the polar end segments are exposed to the water on each side of the membrane.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Protein X floats free in the cytoplasm and is not associated with the membrane at all, because it has polar segments at its ends.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The nonpolar middle segment is exposed to the watery environment outside the cell, and the polar end segments lie in the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All of Protein X lies in the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer, including the polar end segments, because the protein is embedded in the membrane.

stem:
Stimulus: A channel protein in the plasma membrane allows sodium ions to cross the membrane. The protein is embedded in the membrane and forms a pore through it. Researchers compare the R groups of the amino acids that line the pore with the R groups on the outer surface of the protein, where it touches the phospholipid tails.

Question: Which pattern of R groups is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The amino acids that line the pore have nonpolar R groups, and the amino acids on the outer surface have polar or charged R groups.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All of the amino acids have polar or charged R groups, because the channel must let ions cross the membrane.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The amino acids that line the pore have polar or charged R groups, and the amino acids on the outer surface have nonpolar R groups.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All of the amino acids have nonpolar R groups, because the protein is embedded in the hydrophobic interior of the membrane.
